item.title: The Supreme Court First Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Shrank Them: From Flag Salutes to Backpack Searches
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: From refusing to salute the flag to searching backpacks, six rulings gradually mapped the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Court, while declaring that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves," also upheld corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion backpack searches, narrowing the boundaries of those rights.
item.content:encoded:
From refusing to salute the flag to searching backpacks, six rulings gradually mapped the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Court, while declaring that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves," also upheld corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion backpack searches, narrowing the boundaries of those rights.

Each ruling is explained in five or six minutes, covering background and key holdings—ideal for listeners who want to grasp in one go the boundaries of speech, corporal punishment, and backpack searches in American public schools.

5:10 Flag-salute case: student rights enter the schoolhouse
Can students really assert First Amendment rights during class? This case actually began with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families believed saluting the flag violated the commandments against other gods and graven images, so they refused to salute and pledge. In 1940, the Supreme Court ruled against them, and World War II led more districts to require daily salutes and pledges. West Virginia expelled students who refused and listed them as delinquents; parents could be fined or jailed. In 1943, the Court reversed 6–3, with Justice Jackson writing on Flag Day: no official can define orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion, or other opinion; students need not confess words that contradict their hearts or make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students have some First Amendment rights inside school.

11:21 Official prayer struck down as unconstitutional
During the Cold War, America cast itself as a God-fearing nation, adding "Under God" to the Pledge in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951, the New York State Board of Regents asked religious leaders to compose a short, non-denominational prayer, leaving adoption to each district. Districts that used it allowed students to opt out, but parents of ten students sued anyway. In 1962, Engel v. Vitale ruled 6–1 that the prayer was unconstitutional—not because it was mandatory, but because it was composed by the government, which itself constituted an establishment of religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: that the first experiment with our liberties should be a warning; the same power that can establish Christianity to the exclusion of all other religions can also easily establish one sect of Christianity. The decision sparked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families faced ridicule and harassment.

18:31 Armbands are constitutionally protected expression
In December 1965, Des Moines middle and high school students planned to wear black armbands to class to protest U.S. involvement in Vietnam. The school announced in advance that those who refused to remove them would be suspended; some students—including four siblings—wore them and were suspended. In 1969, the Supreme Court ruled 7–2 for the students. The issue was not ordinary dress code but a quiet, passive expression akin to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Without evidence of actual or reasonably foreseeable material disruption of schoolwork, school officials may not suppress student opinion. The opinion declared that public schools are not totalitarian enclaves, and students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This "substantial disruption" test became the benchmark for campus speech. Justice Black dissented, predicting students would defy nearly all rules; the hosts note that this slippery-slope argument sounds quite absurd.

24:40 School-funded newspaper can be censored
In 1983, Hazelwood East High School's student newspaper, The Spectrum, had two articles that unsettled Principal Reynolds: one on teenage pregnancy used pseudonyms but might still identify the interviewee, and a divorce story named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to delete the entire two pages rather than just the articles, citing lack of time to edit and the need to publish before semester's end. In 1988, the Supreme Court ruled 5–3 for the school. The key distinction was between "tolerating student speech" and "promoting student speech": the paper was funded by the school, readers would assume the school endorsed its content, and the two pieces were indeed immature in journalistic ethics. The Court held that schools may regulate content they promote. This carved the first clear boundary around the rights established in Tinker.

29:46 Corporal punishment is not cruel and unusual
Host Tracy suddenly recalled that many teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks when she was young, and research showed corporal punishment has not disappeared in America. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's regulation paddle was less than two feet long, three or four inches wide, and half an inch thick, with one to five strokes per incident; but Ingram was hit more than 20 times in a single incident and required medical attention. The Court did not dwell on whether this particular case was excessive; it ruled that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The Eighth Amendment protects convicted persons, and prisoners are separated from schoolchildren by the "harsh facts of criminal conviction and incarceration"; schools are open places with teachers and peers as witnesses, and students can go home after school. According to NEA statistics, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually used in 14; boys, Black students, and students with disabilities are paddled at significantly higher rates.

33:52 Backpack search only needs reasonable suspicion
In 1980, a 14-year-old New Jersey student, TLO, was reported by a teacher for smoking in the restroom. Vice Principal Choplik searched her purse, found cigarettes and rolling papers, then continued searching and found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing. TLO was convicted and sentenced to one year of probation. In 1985, the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that the search was legal. The Court acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment binds school officials and that students have a legitimate expectation of privacy, but it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. Therefore, school searches need not meet the probable cause standard required of police; they only need the lower threshold of reasonable suspicion. The teacher's report gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and the purse was the obvious place; seeing rolling papers naturally extended the suspicion to marijuana, which was also reasonable.

item.title: Criticism That Lands: Give High Standards and Trust First
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.description: Criticism is accepted not because you soften it with praise, but because the other person sees: the bar is high, and you believe they can reach it. In the experiment, a single sentence — "the standards are high but you can meet them" — drove Black students' revision rates to the highest.
item.content:encoded:
Criticism is accepted not because you soften it with praise, but because the other person sees: the bar is high, and you believe they can reach it. In the experiment, a single sentence — "the standards are high but you can meet them" — drove Black students' revision rates to the highest.

The originator of stereotype threat research breaks down the mechanism and lands the intervention in a replicable experimental script. Twenty minutes of dense information, no generic communication platitudes.

1:04 Identity bias makes you choke in the moment
When a situation carries a negative label about one of your identities, and the situation matters to you, you worry about being judged by that label. That worry comes from the situation itself; it immediately depresses performance on tests, sports, or intellectual tasks, and over time makes people avoid such situations, shaping who they befriend, where they live, and where they send their kids to school. The anxiety comes not from ability but from the expectation of being defined by a label.

3:10 Social media corners you with labels
Social media's power lies in rapidly spreading caricatures of groups; people have no patience for nuance or exceptions, so it naturally multiplies the situations where you feel "I'll be seen through my identity." It occasionally spreads images that reduce threat, but the overall tone is negative. The result: in a diverse society, everyone is more vigilant about their identity and what others might think.

6:16 A 15-minute self-reflection can lift grades
In racially integrated classrooms, Black students constantly carry the possibility of being underestimated. Teachers asked seventh graders to spend 15 minutes writing a short essay about the people and things they value most. White students were barely affected, but Black students used the chance to signal to the teacher "I'm more than that label," and their grades began to rise, feeding a positive loop: higher grades → less vigilance about the label → higher grades. The intervention costs almost nothing, yet it changes long-term trajectories.

9:20 In diverse settings, the vigilance: remember or forget
The author calls this state churn. When people from different identity backgrounds work together and the outcome matters, you oscillate between two choices: remember "others may read me through my group's stereotype" to protect yourself, or forget it and relax into trusting the people in front of you. This is not fragility; it is real situational pressure. When the stakes are high, it constantly drains attention that should go to the task.

12:24 High standards plus trust make feedback stick
In the experiment, students wrote an essay about their favorite teacher and received critical feedback. Two delivery styles — direct feedback, or a "positive high hat" first — were trusted by White students but highly distrusted by Black students. A third style added just one sentence: "We have high standards because this essay will be published; I've read yours and believe you can meet them." Under that condition, Black students took the essay home to revise at three times the rate of the other conditions.

14:26 Never assume others already trust you
Having served as dean and provost for years, Claude believes the most useful ability is realizing that every person you work with needs that respect signal. Society's common mistake is assuming trust already exists, but in reality, people worry about how you view the group they belong to. Truly effective leaders are good at sending this signal first: even if employees disagree with a decision, if they feel respected as people and for their potential, the team atmosphere changes completely.

17:35 Let people see you as human before trust
Claude breaks good communication into three things: first, let the other person know you understand what the situation means to them; when power is unequal, the higher-status person must release a safety signal first. Second, near-paranoid clarity — beating around the bush destroys valuable information. Third, warmth and goodwill — people need to confirm you are a good person before they hand over trust. Matt sums it up as connection, clarity, and care.

item.title: Latin Won't Train a Surgeon: Make Exams Hard, Not Just Useless
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-econtalk-拉丁文练不出外科医生-考试难-不如考得有用/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-econtalk-拉丁文练不出外科医生-考试难-不如考得有用/
item.description: Latin won't train a surgeon: skills barely transfer. If you believe 'the harder, the better for the brain,' a nation's brightest will be wasted on the most useless knowledge—that's the lesson of the Qing dynasty civil exams.
item.content:encoded:
Latin won't train a surgeon: skills barely transfer. If you believe 'the harder, the better for the brain,' a nation's brightest will be wasted on the most useless knowledge—that's the lesson of the Qing dynasty civil exams.

Putting imperial civil exams, military selection, and modern transfer experiments on the same chain of evidence is a rare move that bridges history and talent assessment, and the two sides genuinely clash.

10:03 Wrong exam content dooms even smart candidates
Hong Xiuquan failed the Qing imperial exams at least four times. After his last failure, on the road home he had visions, came to believe he was Christ's younger brother, and eventually launched the Taiping Rebellion—which Daisy says may be the deadliest civil war in human history, with deaths possibly around thirty million. The losers weren't just Hong: exam slots were far fewer than the candidate pool, and many kept trying into their forties and fifties without passing, their only way home being teaching. Daisy adds that the deeper cost fell on those who passed: they mastered the eight-legged essay but knew nothing of the science and mathematics then changing the world. When the brightest young minds can only drill a rigid format, a country bleeds in two directions at once.

22:51 British civil service reform was elite self-replication
The Northcote-Trevelyan Report is often seen by Britons as the founding document of the modern civil service, but Daisy backs the revisionist view: under the banner of a unified exam, it pushed Oxford and Cambridge classics graduates into key posts. Benjamin Jowett, Master of Balliol, worked behind the scenes to place his classics students throughout the empire. Michael Coolican's 'No Tradesmen and No Women' argues that the 1854 report reduced the crudest buying and selling of offices but also snuffed out the professional exams that departments had been developing. Exams aren't the problem; what they test determines whether they select for merit or for people like the selectors.

35:58 Bureaucracies without price signals correct via corpses
Daisy attributes bureaucratic failure to a lack of feedback: no price mechanism, no profit and loss, so departments can't know if their plans save or harm people. The military might seem a counterexample, but military bureaucracies err constantly in peacetime; Britain, after nearly every long peace, stumbled into crisis in the first year of war—the shell crisis of WWI being one example. What forces correction isn't internal inspection but mass death on the battlefield. She calls it a more brutal correction mechanism than prices. To make bureaucracies reliable, you first need a signal that makes consequences visible; otherwise, no matter how rigorous the exam, it can't save the quality of everyday decisions.

43:06 The Royal Navy won by testing navigation, not Latin
Daisy reminds us that in Victorian times, Britain's real pillar wasn't the army but the Royal Navy. As early as 1677, after successive defeats by the Dutch, Samuel Pepys introduced an oral exam for lieutenants: three senior officers grilled candidates on how to command a ship. Over the next century-plus, skills like navigation, chart-making, and trigonometry entered written exams; Nelson, Cook, Flinders, and Bligh—all chart-makers—passed through this gate. Daisy uses this to contrast two exam traditions: Pepys tested skills needed immediately; Macaulay and Northcote-Trevelyan later wanted classical languages. One was for safe sailing, the other for class distinction—so the outcomes naturally differed.

47:31 Content irrelevant? Macaulay's screening theory misses a key link
Here's the highlight: Daisy reads aloud Macaulay's 1833 parliamentary speech. In essence: whatever a generation teaches, the top performers will inevitably be the smartest, most diligent, and most honor-seeking of the youth; so Cambridge could teach Ptolemy instead of Newton and its best students would still be excellent; teach Cherokee instead of Greek, and the best Cherokee speakers would still be outstanding; even astrology and alchemy would do. Another MP praised it on the spot as the most practical speech in parliamentary history, but Daisy bluntly says it's more like a man carried away by his own eloquence, completely missing that 'what you learn really matters.'

51:21 Dead branches and corn: wrong content makes discipline wasted water
Daisy uses American medical educator Abraham Flexner's 1917 rebuttal to close out Macaulay. Flexner said proponents of mental discipline are like Egyptian priests: they stick a row of dead branches in the soil and then water them on schedule for discipline's sake. If you planted corn, you'd get the same discipline plus a harvest. In contrast, American medical schools of the time forced aspiring doctors to study Greek and Latin before touching medical books. Flexner's answer: medicine itself is hard enough; using it to train the mind is far more efficient than using dead languages. Daisy agrees: spending the best years of the most talented on discredited or useless knowledge only benefits rivals who teach their youth real knowledge.

59:21 Rectangles don't train triangles: transfer needs identical elements
Thorndike designed a cleaner controlled experiment: have people practice estimating rectangle areas until they improve markedly, then test them on triangle areas—transfer is almost nil. If even two such similar shapes don't transfer, the claim that classical languages sharpen the mind is even less credible. Thorndike's explanation was identical elements: transfer occurs only when old and new tasks share common components; far transfer largely breaks down. Daisy derives a design principle for exams: to select navigators, test navigation and trigonometry; to select doctors, test medicine. Effective exams connect difficulty directly to real tasks.

item.title: Global Liquidity Peaks: The More Aggressively You Spent on AI in H1, the Sooner You Get Discounted
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.description: A stock market rally needs new money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that most aggressively invested in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
item.content:encoded:
A stock market rally needs new money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that most aggressively invested in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.

Explaining US AI capex, Hong Kong IPO demand, and household balance sheets on the same funding chain offers a macro framework that doesn't treat AI as a panacea.

0:33 Low IPO break rate is not a good sign
Don't take the low break rate of Hong Kong IPOs as a sign of market strength. In the first half of this year, the break rate was only around 10-20%, far below the roughly 50-50 normal level under a market-driven mechanism, meaning the participants were mainly short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently, the supply of new listings has decreased, and some IPO-related funds have had problems, but the two newly listed companies still broke issue price, showing that temporary supply-side controls haven't solved the fundamental issue: Hong Kong also faces peaking liquidity.

12:07 The more aggressive the AI spending, the sooner the punishment
Market sentiment reversed within a quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI capex talk, the higher the valuation. By the end of July, when half-year reports were released, any major internet company that had made aggressive capital expenditures in H1—especially those that burned through free cash flow—was discounted, and even Google wasn't exempt. Q2 was the most FOMO quarter across the supply chain; everyone rushed to spend before prices rose, and inventory still supported gross margins. By Q3, with inventory depleted and price increases taking effect, the adverse factors will appear together.

15:54 Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing shape. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco introduced leasing-to-own to help customers finance purchases, recognizing future revenue as sales upfront; Nvidia is now also pushing leasing-to-own. In its earnings report, free cash flow fell by half quarter-over-quarter, and accounts receivable are far above historical levels—possibly partly related to the credit enhancement and payment structure from leasing-to-own. So Nvidia may have reached a point where it needs more aggressive financial measures to sustain capital market expectations, similar to Cisco's situation back then.

33:21 Primary market money comes from bullets three years ago
The answer lies in fund raising timing. The money concentrated in AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022; from 2023 to 2025 they barely invested, until they saw state capital placing bets when no one dared and making the most money—the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, two large language models, and two major chip companies stimulated market-based funds. The mentality is: copy the state's playbook. So this is not a rational long-term increment, but more like a delayed emotional release.

47:31 New property policy removes households from the funding chain
The key of recent property policy is not to rescue developers but to detach households from the old financing cycle. In the past, buying pre-sold homes meant households played the role of financing objects in the investment-driven chain: paying first, receiving the home later. The policy pushes the chain toward marketization, so buyers get completed homes and only act as consumers, with risk reset to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when home prices were near the bottom, aiming to stabilize the denominator of the asset side first, avoiding panic from breaking the chain during a decline. Japan after the 1990s and China's coal and mining industry consolidation followed similar paths.

1:01:34 Slow bull is not a slogan but a chip structure
A slow bull doesn't rely on slogans but on layering market chips by duration: at the bottom are low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips held by insurers as long-term money that rarely trades; above that are public funds and index funds, serving a quasi-stabilizing function; China Securities Finance and Central Huijin adjust the index at a higher level; at the top are retail investors, private funds, and active management money. New insurance regulations require liabilities and assets to match in duration, yield, and liquidity, institutionally ensuring long money for long-term investment, medium money for medium-term, and short money for short-term—not allowing short-term household money to be invested in ten-year illiquid assets.

1:22:49 Crises grow bigger with each bailout; at least one and a half bubbles
Since the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks have become increasingly accustomed to directly intervening in crises by printing money, with each action faster than the last. Quantitative easing after 2008 should have been cleared during the rate hike cycle, but was interrupted by political intervention, and then COVID hit in 2020, so another larger wave of easing was layered on before the previous bubble had dissipated—today we have at least one and a half bubbles accumulated. Central bank governors have learned to print even more money immediately when a crisis appears, with the endogenous result of inflation, financial asset appreciation, and wealth disparity all intensifying simultaneously. As long as bubbles are not allowed to clear, the world may face some form of prolonged stagflation.

item.title: Central Banks Won't Kill the $100 Bill: It's a $2.5 Trillion Interest-Free Loan
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.description: Cash use is declining, yet the dollar in circulation is at a record high. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: this money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, at the cost of enabling global money launderers.
item.content:encoded:
Cash use is declining, yet the dollar in circulation is at a record high. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: this money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, at the cost of enabling global money launderers.

This episode breaks down money laundering from 'bank wire transfers' to watches, tractors, casino chips, and VAT loopholes, and explains why central banks are reluctant to abolish the $100 bill.

5:09 Money laundering scale hasn't changed in 30 years
The most commonly cited estimate for money laundering is 2% to 5% of global GDP annually, which at today's roughly $100 trillion GDP would be $2 trillion to $5 trillion. This figure comes from a rough estimate by former IMF chief Michel Camdessus in the late 1990s, and no one has since provided a better answer. Oliver reminds us that what should be more alarming is that this ratio hasn't changed in 30 years: decades of anti-money laundering efforts haven't shrunk the criminal economy; they've only barely kept it from growing faster than the overall economy.

9:10 Banks spend $200 billion a year on AML with near-zero effect
Banks complaining about KYC costs isn't just whining. The 1970 Bank Secrecy Act in the U.S. and the 1989 FATF global standards forced banks to hire compliance teams and install AI monitoring software. LexisNexis estimates global AML compliance costs around $200 billion a year—enough to end world hunger and provide clean water to everyone. But the system generates massive numbers of suspicious activity reports, and launderers still stay ahead of regulators. The problem isn't that banks aren't trying; it's that the whole system is costly, has weak feedback, and almost no one is held accountable for results.

12:14 Trade-based laundering is an order of magnitude larger than cash smuggling
Cash smuggling makes bank-based laundering look small, but the bigger chunk doesn't involve money at all: value is hidden in goods. Mexico receives about $25 billion in cash annually, while U.S. exports of John Deere and Caterpillar equipment become the counterpart for drug cartels; European luxury goods flow to China, and from China drugs and goods are imported, with triangular trade settled through misinvoicing. Global Financial Integrity estimates trade-based laundering at about $1 trillion a year. A million-dollar watch worn through customs is far easier than moving a million in cash.

17:18 The Vancouver model: Chinese cash demand meets drug cash supply
China's每人每年 only $50,000 forex conversion quota, but wealthy Chinese have large spending needs abroad. The Vancouver model matches this demand with drug cartels' dollar cash supply: cash bags are handed to Chinese gamblers outside Canadian casinos, the money is lost at the tables, and the gamblers owe a debt. That debt is offset by renminbi transactions on the Chinese side and subsequent drug sales. Viewed alone, the gambling looks like a loss; across the whole chain, it's a triangular settlement that simultaneously repatriates drug funds and moves Chinese capital out. The model has since expanded globally, with luxury goods, daily necessities, and drugs all serving as value carriers.

23:25 VAT loophole lets the same goods repeatedly extract 20%
The EU's zero-rated cross-border transactions were meant to avoid tax authorities checking each other, but they became an ATM: goods entering the UK from Ireland don't incur VAT, and when sold to a related shell company, 20% is added; that shell exports the goods back to Ireland and claims a refund from the UK tax authority for the 20% it never paid. The cycle repeats, hence the name carousel fraud. The UK largely suppressed it with multi-agency crackdowns, but fraudsters moved to the continent, where it now amounts to about €50 billion a year, spreading from Lithuania to Portugal. Criminal organizations have no upper limit on competition: the more they cooperate, the bigger they get.

27:27 No one uses cash, yet central banks print record amounts
In the digital payment era, cash transactions are only about 9% in the UK and 13% in the US, so paper currency supply should logically shrink. After Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey articulated the banknote paradox in 2009, the phenomenon intensified: UK currency in circulation doubled, and the US is close to $2.5 trillion. Central banks' explanation of 'store of value' doesn't hold—surveys show the average American adult has only a few hundred dollars on hand, while per capita currency in circulation exceeds $7,000. The Fed estimates about 65% of US banknotes are abroad, but that just pushes the question across borders: no one knows who actually holds these notes.

32:31 The $100 bill is a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the government
Seigniorage isn't simply profit from printing money: a $100 bill costs 9 cents to produce, but it isn't 'sold' to you—you can redeem it for goods at face value anytime, so public cash holdings are essentially an interest-free loan. With nearly $2.5 trillion in circulation, the U.S. government gets interest-free funds equivalent to about 6% of its debt; federal interest payments are about 19% of the budget, and if that $2.5 trillion had to pay interest, it would add about another percentage point. That's why central banks don't want to hear about abolishing the bill.

47:51 AML incentives are inverted: more reports, less crime enforcement
Suspicious activity reports were meant to be real-time intelligence for law enforcement, but reality is the opposite: banks hire thousands of compliance officers to file reports, law enforcement lacks resources to read them, and most reports go into a black hole. Banks can be fined billions for missing a report, but there's no reward for doing it right. Side effects include debanking—many suspected individuals, often Muslims, get cut off from financial institutions. The guests' solution isn't more compliance officers but generating fewer reports, actually reading them, and genuinely prosecuting financial criminals to raise the cost of laundering, rather than drowning everyone in paperwork.

item.title: Russia Is Stuck in Ukraine but Still Has the Strength to Open a New Front Against NATO
