item.description: ResNet is the most cited paper of the 21st century, but its real contribution isn't deepening networks—it's the residual stream, a working memory that lets models store and edit information, fundamentally changing our understanding of neural networks.
item.content:encoded:
ResNet is the most cited paper of the 21st century, but its real contribution isn't deepening networks—it's the residual stream, a working memory that lets models store and edit information, fundamentally changing our understanding of neural networks.

This episode uses clear animations and experiments to explain why residual connections work, how they led to Transformers, and evidence for the residual stream as working memory. Ideal for anyone wanting to deeply understand the essence of modern AI architectures.

2:07 Deeper networks performed worse
In early 2015, Kaiming He's team used careful initialization to push networks to 30 layers, but performance was worse than 14 layers (error rate 16.59% vs 13.34%). Theoretically, a 30-layer model could achieve at least the same performance as a 14-layer one via identity mapping, but optimizers couldn't find such solutions. This hinted the problem wasn't network capacity but the training process itself.

15:18 Shattered gradients are the root cause
Through loss landscape visualization, they found that as layers increased, the loss surface for early layers became extremely rugged, and gradient directions were as random as white noise—this was called the 'shattered gradients problem.' Gradients are the core signal for learning; once they fail, deep networks cannot train effectively.

17:18 Residual connections: an almost absurdly simple fix
Kaiming He's team's solution was laughably simple: between every two layers, add the input tensor directly to the output, creating a skip connection. This provided a direct path for activations and gradients, effectively eliminating the shattered gradients problem. With skip connections, a 74-layer network's accuracy jumped from 38.9% to 72.6%, sweeping major vision competitions in 2015.

20:19 ResNets upended hierarchical representation theory
A Cornell team found that deleting or even shuffling layers of a ResNet had little impact on performance. This contradicted the then-dominant hierarchical representation theory, which held that each layer builds on the previous one, so removing any layer should be catastrophic. This forced the field to rethink: ResNets might not be learning hierarchical features but iteratively refining a 'residual stream' running through the network.

26:26 The residual stream: modern AI's hidden backbone
Straightening the skip connections reveals an uninterrupted stream from input to output, with each layer making incremental modifications. This 'residual stream' later became the core design of Transformers and the foundation of modern AI. However, subsequent research showed that ResNets learn both hierarchical representations and refine the residual stream—they can coexist.

29:28 The residual stream is the model's working memory
Meta's team found that in vision Transformers, certain positions in the residual stream have unusually large activations, concentrated in image regions that are not important. They hypothesized the model uses these positions as 'registers' to aggregate global information. Experiments confirmed: embedding vectors from these high-activation positions performed remarkably in image classification (85.2% vs 10.8%), and adding extra 'register tokens' meant the model no longer used image positions.

item.title: Fed Credibility Shatters, Options Market Shrugs
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-excessreturns-美联储信誉崩塌-期权市场却当无事发生/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-excessreturns-美联储信誉崩塌-期权市场却当无事发生/
item.description: The Fed's credibility broke over a single skipped hike, yet the options market prices meeting days like any other—the cheapest insurance may be an illusion.
item.content:encoded:
The Fed's credibility broke over a single skipped hike, yet the options market prices meeting days like any other—the cheapest insurance may be an illusion.

Three pieces of evidence—sticky inflation, midterm elections, and Fed credibility—point to the same conclusion: volatility is too low, and cheap protection is a mirage. The framework and data are concrete.

3:03 A Fed Without Forward Guidance Is Flipping a Coin
The hosts open by noting the shift: at past meetings, markets knew the odds with high certainty, but this time the probability of a hike at the next meeting is only 55-45, barely better than a coin toss. Add Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks about phasing out forward guidance, and every meeting could become 'see the result, then react.' Rate surprises transmit through debt and leverage to all assets, so volatility needs repricing. The hosts also assert from history: once truly tested by markets, nearly every official eventually caves, so the current promise of 'never pre-empting market expectations' is itself the variable most worth testing.

17:31 Midterm Election Volatility Priced as an Ordinary Day
Kevin Muir argues that midterm election volatility is severely underpriced. During the 2022 midterms, options priced a ±1.8% one-day move in the S&P on voting day; in 2018 it was ±1.25%; now it's only ±0.9%. And this time Trump's approval is at historic lows, and he just spent a prime-time hour talking about 'election fraud,' seemingly laying groundwork to challenge the result. Muir notes: even if you think he's overreacting, it doesn't matter—as voting day approaches, the question of whether the election will be contested will itself be repriced. With volatility near seasonal lows and implied correlation at historic lows, the odds for long volatility are much better than usual.

23:41 Disinflation Is a Supply Illusion; Demand Hasn't Cooled
Ahan Manon splits PCE components into 'demand-driven' and 'supply-driven.' Their contributions are now 3.31 vs. 0.38; even if you strip out the energy supply shock from Iran entirely, the remaining demand side alone is enough to keep inflation above the Fed's 2% target. Historically, demand-driven inflation is slow and persistent, while supply-driven inflation tends to spike quickly and mean-revert within 6 to 12 months. More troubling is the breadth: in recent months, 70% to 80% of PCE components are rising faster than 2%. June saw a negative month-over-month print and July only rebounded 16 basis points, but these short-term cool-offs are almost entirely from the supply side; the demand-driven trend hasn't been interrupted.

34:51 One Hike Could Have Fixed Credibility; He Didn't Do It
Ben Hunt says Warsh hit a 'self-goal' at the post-July-FOMC press conference. The newcomer's debut and hawkish inflation talk had repaired the 'Fed credibility' narrative substantially; but the real move was to hike 25 basis points immediately. One hike would have convinced markets he means what he says, and no repeated hikes would be needed. Skipping that step reversed the narrative completely: every independent report in the financial press that week said the same thing in different words—'meet the new boss, same as the old boss.' Credibility, once broken, is hard to glue back; August's gold rally is the market's reaction to 'hawkish talk, no action.'

40:13 After the Credibility Hit, Only Jawboning Financial Repression Remains
Ben Hunt lists four pressures the Fed and Treasury must manage but cannot let blow up: the Iran war has no easy exit and oil stays higher for longer; fiscal stimulus fades and tariff pressures return; the insurance sector has a systemic problem with captive insurers being used to take on private investments; and the 10- and 30-year long end cannot be allowed to rise. Any one could be the fuse for the next financial crisis. Handling these requires credibility, which was just wounded, so all policy options reduce to 'jawboning financial repression'—using statements and intervention to cap yields rather than letting markets price them. His judgment: this operation has no maturity date and will only accelerate.

49:25 Options Market Treats Fed Meetings as Ordinary Days
Brent Kachuba shows an options term structure with almost no event risk: the 0DTE straddle on the day of Warsh's speech is worth only 38 index points; SPX options expiring August 31 have implied volatility of just 7%, the overall term structure is at 90-day lows, and put open interest is low. He usually avoids trading Fed events because events turn options into a 'tax'—premium is collected before the event, and time value decays once it passes. But the special thing this time is that the market has compressed volatility expectations to near zero, and no one is hedging. He bought cheap short-term put spreads before Jackson Hole as a 'lottery ticket,' because if Warsh says one thing the market doesn't like, naked option sellers will get squeezed instantly. After the event passes, that's a better time to follow directional trends.

58:42 Outsourcing Writing to AI Outsources Thinking Too
The closing topic is Druckenmiller's WSJ op-ed: he publicly said it was written by AI, with the simple reason that AI writes better than he does. The hosts argue the core question is whether the views and emotions belong to the author; Druckenmiller's piece reads like his usual gut judgments, with AI only organizing and expressing, so it's not deceptive. Ben Hunt draws the line at writing itself: writing is part of the thinking process—'I write to figure out what I think.' When the text-generation step is outsourced, readers lose an important clue: whether the author actually thought through these words. Obvious AI products are already flooding investment blogs; to judge whether an opinion is reliable, don't just look at how polished the prose is—ask whether the view has a thinking process behind it.

item.title: China's Economic Peak Has Passed: Credit Dries Up, Deflation Looms
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-geopoliticsdec-中国经济巅峰已过-美国优势还将扩大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-geopoliticsdec-中国经济巅峰已过-美国优势还将扩大/
item.description: China's share of global GDP peaked in 2021 and has been declining since; credit growth has fallen from 18% to 5%, and real growth may be only 1.5%-2%; the U.S. has outperformed for five consecutive years. The narrative of industrial chain dominance is disproven by data; the future looks more like Japan-style deflation.
item.content:encoded:
China's share of global GDP peaked in 2021 and has been declining since; credit growth has fallen from 18% to 5%, and real growth may be only 1.5%-2%; the U.S. has outperformed for five consecutive years. The narrative of industrial chain dominance is disproven by data; the future looks more like Japan-style deflation.

To counter the mainstream narrative that 'China's new industries = growth engine,' grounding judgments in verifiable data on credit, special bonds, and demographics; for those looking to update their long-term U.S.-China outlook.

0:05 China has missed its window to overtake the U.S.
Dmitri sets the tone with official data: China's share of global GDP peaked at 18.5% in 2021 and has declined each year since; the U.S. has risen from 24% to about 26%. He concludes that China has almost no chance of replacing the U.S. as the world's largest economy, and the U.S. economic advantage may continue to widen over the next decade. Logan fully agrees and steers the discussion toward a 'decline, not collapse' framework.

2:11 The root of China's slowdown is the end of credit expansion
Logan attributes China's slowdown to the end of extraordinary credit expansion. After the financial crisis, China added credit equivalent to one-third of global GDP in eight years; credit growth fell from an average of 18% in 2007-2016 to 9% after 2017, and now stands at just over 5%. Once credit stops, borrowers can't refinance, and investment decelerates. Official figures still report 5.2% growth in 2023 and 5% in 2024 and 2025, but he estimates real growth since 2022 has been only 1.5%-2%, already below the U.S.

6:14 Using purchasing power parity rewards deflation
Addressing the common rebuttal that 'China has already surpassed the U.S. in PPP terms,' Logan says PPP comparisons are still meaningful for developing countries but don't hold up between the world's two largest economies: scoring by PPP rewards China for producing deflation—the lower domestic prices are, the stronger the economy looks, yet deflation is precisely the problem. He also stresses that debt is repaid in nominal local currency, so nominal GDP matters; and the exchange rate is not an exogenous variable but an external signal of China's policy capacity.

13:25 Capital controls are not a cure, only a time-buyer
Logan concedes that China's capital controls are effective, but argues they are not a panacea for massive macro imbalances. The impossible trinity dictates that free capital flow, exchange rate stability, and monetary policy independence can only be achieved two at a time. The function of capital controls is to slow outflows, suppress rapid cross-border volatility, and channel outflows into government-visible avenues—Huawei and BYD can go global aggressively, while private firms like HNA in 2016 had their overseas acquisitions halted; this is the two sides of the same screening mechanism.

17:35 Credit still subsidizes old industries, not new ones
Logan rebuts the claim that 'credit is shifting to more productive new industries': central bank data show that the share of loans issued at or below the Loan Prime Rate has risen from over 20% to 59%, indicating banks are continuously subsidizing. The share of special revenue bonds directed to so-called strategic industries rose only from about 2% in 2021 to 6% in 2025; the vast majority still flows to traditional sectors. Using the 2023 input-output table, he estimates that electric vehicles, batteries, AI, solar, etc., together account for about 6.3% of GDP, while the decline in real estate and infrastructure investment is about six times the increase from these new industries.

27:45 Europe is the last buyer of China's excess capacity
Logan judges that if Europe turns protectionist, China will be 'truly finished': the U.S. market has narrowed and transshipment space is limited, and the developing world cannot absorb China's excess capacity while maintaining its own growth. He warns that the U.S. is wrong to focus only on the bilateral deficit—the deficit is determined by the savings-investment gap; tariffs only redistribute the deficit, and not addressing the underlying imbalance will only spawn more transshipment trade.

34:58 Without touching taxes, domestic demand won't take off
Logan draws a parallel with Soviet Premier Kosygin's reforms: Brezhnev chose to pivot to a technological revolution rather than push reforms that would undermine ideology. For China to convert savings into consumption, the real lever is tax policy—extracting resources from high-net-worth individuals, state-owned enterprises, and private firms excluded from the financial system. But he thinks it is almost inconceivable that Xi Jinping would go on TV and announce that 'the fiscal and financial system of the past 15 years is no longer applicable'; Beijing's insistence on the 5% growth narrative is partly to undermine export controls and discourage Western investment in alternative supply chains.

39:00 China in 2035 will look like Japan today
Logan predicts that without major policy shifts, China's economy in 2035 will resemble Japan's: persistent deflation, persistent external surpluses, currency depreciation pressure, and low interest rates. The hardest constraint is demographics—China's actual average age at death is 73, and the early PRC baby boom will bring a population decline of 50-60 million over the next decade, about 3%-4% of the total population; even maintaining the low birth rate of 7.92 million last year won't stop it. He also notes that the fiscal deficit is already close to $2 trillion per year, about 9.5% of GDP, leaving far fewer resources available than in the past. Finally, he says that if China truly wins by export share, it will invite stronger political backlash—'winning is losing.'

item.title: Bell Used Einstein's Own Tools to Refute His Central Claim
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-theoriesofever-贝尔用爱因斯坦自己的工具推翻了他的核心论点/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-theoriesofever-贝尔用爱因斯坦自己的工具推翻了他的核心论点/
item.category: Theories of Everything with Curt Jaimungal
item.description: The EPR argument forces a choice between an incomplete quantum description and action at a distance; determinism is never an assumption but a conclusion that is inferred. The full logic of Bell's theorem must start here.
item.content:encoded:
The EPR argument forces a choice between an incomplete quantum description and action at a distance; determinism is never an assumption but a conclusion that is inferred. The full logic of Bell's theorem must start here.

Maudlin traces the story from Einstein's 1905 photoelectric effect paper to Bell's 1964 inequality, breaking the EPR argument into steps that can be checked one by one. For those who want to truly understand nonlocality rather than memorize conclusions.

3:05 The father of quantum theory is not Planck but Einstein
Although Planck is usually regarded as the father of quantum theory, it was Einstein's 1905 photoelectric effect paper that actually proposed the quantization hypothesis. Planck only did statistical calculations, while Einstein explicitly argued that energy is transferred in discrete quanta. Maudlin deliberately corrects this historical attribution.

45:32 A single particle is enough to force action at a distance
Einstein's objection at the 1927 Solvay Conference was: if the wave function completely describes a single particle, and the wave spreads in all directions toward the screen, then the particle could produce effects at multiple locations simultaneously. To avoid multiple points of action, one must introduce an instantaneous and global collapse mechanism of the wave function—this is action at a distance. Note that this is not about superluminal signaling.

1:14:50 If the wave function is real, locality has no place to reside
The wave function of a many-particle system is defined on configuration space, not physical space; for example, a two-particle system is a six-dimensional configuration space. In classical mechanics, configuration space is a mathematical convenience, but if the wave function is taken as fundamental reality, configuration space becomes the physical stage, and the definition of local forces in each small spatial region becomes problematic. This is another layer of Einstein's concern about dynamical locality.

1:31:59 The EPR reality criterion cannot be coherently denied
The EPR reality criterion says: if, without disturbing a system, one can predict with probability 1 the value of a physical quantity, then that quantity corresponds to an element of physical reality. Maudlin emphasizes that this is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one. He refutes common attempts to deny the criterion, arguing that it is analytic and cannot be coherently denied. This sets the stage for the subsequent either-or conclusion.

2:02:26 Either the description is incomplete, or accept action at a distance
Because the reality criterion cannot be denied, the EPR argument forces a choice: either accept that the quantum description is incomplete, or accept that Alice's operation in her lab indeed disturbs the physical state of Bob's particle—that is, action at a distance. Einstein found action at a distance absurd, so he chose incompleteness. This is the logical exit of the entire EPR argument.

2:10:34 Denying determinism does not escape Bell's conclusion
Maudlin repeatedly emphasizes that in the EPR argument determinism is not assumed but inferred from perfect correlations and locality. He quotes Bell's own words: 'Insofar as determinism plays a role in the EPR argument, it is not assumed but inferred.' Therefore, attempts to escape Bell's conclusion by denying determinism are completely ineffective.

2:43:53 Bohr's famous response was understood by no one
Faced with the EPR argument, Bohr had only two logically possible responses: accept action at a distance, or admit that the quantum description is incomplete. But Bohr chose neither. Maudlin says his response paper is 'a mess' that no one can understand. He even mentions that in the book edited by Wheeler and Zurek, two pages of Bohr's article are in reversed order, yet no one noticed because no one could follow the logic anyway.

2:55:02 Any local theory gives wrong predictions
Bell's starting point was precisely the EPR paper, but his conclusion was that Einstein's fundamental claim about 'no action at a distance' was wrong: any local theory fails to make correct predictions. Maudlin calls this a great ironic reversal—Bell used Einstein's own tools to refute his fundamental claim. This is the true entry point for understanding why Bell's theorem matters.

item.title: The Quantum Endgame Is Not About Cleaner Qubits, It's About Who Can Mass-Produce with Phone Chip Lines
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-fromfirstprinc-硅自旋将赢-百万比特只需一块硅晶圆/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-fromfirstprinc-硅自旋将赢-百万比特只需一块硅晶圆/
item.description: The endgame of quantum computing is not about whose qubits are cleaner, but about who can mass-produce using existing semiconductor fabs; silicon spin qubits reuse TSMC lithography, while ion traps are stuck with a hundred thousand laser beams and superconductors with warehouse-sized refrigerators.
item.content:encoded:
The endgame of quantum computing is not about whose qubits are cleaner, but about who can mass-produce using existing semiconductor fabs; silicon spin qubits reuse TSMC lithography, while ion traps are stuck with a hundred thousand laser beams and superconductors with warehouse-sized refrigerators.

The exclusive value is in the second half: HRL paper's CNOT error rate, AI auto-tuning, and FFP's striking scores; the first half's principle explanations are more introductory, and veterans can fast-forward.

0:00 Ion traps and superconductors need miracles first; silicon doesn't
To build an ion trap with a hundred thousand qubits, you'd first need to invent the optical miracle of a hundred thousand laser beams; for a million superconducting qubits, you'd need a cryostat the size of a warehouse; a million spin qubits only require standard 300mm silicon wafers, run through the same lithography equipment that TSMC, ASML, and Intel use to make phone processors. Krishna uses this to set the tone for the whole episode: the key to the quantum race is not single-qubit fidelity, but whether the path to scale already exists within the industrial system.

32:48 Quantum computing is no longer about principles, but about engineering
In 2000, DiVincenzo proposed five criteria, aiming to dismiss liquid-state NMR quantum computing. In this episode, FFP proposes its own three criteria: qubit quality, control, and scalability with economics. The rest of the episode scores four routes—superconducting, ion trap, neutral atom, and silicon spin—item by item. Laying out the evaluation system itself tells you: quantum computing has entered the stage of engineering competition, and you can't just talk about principles.

1:24:33 Superconducting isn't a technical failure, it's an engineering impossibility
Estimates show that a thousand logical qubits would require ten million transmon physical qubits. Control line count is limited by the cooling capacity of dilution refrigerators, frequency crowding occurs, and helium-3 supply becomes a new resource constraint. FFP gives superconducting only 1/10 on scalability and economics, with a total score of 11/30. This is the first time the episode separates 'technically strong' from 'engineering infeasible'; a warehouse-sized refrigerator means even data centers might not fit it.

1:47:08 Ion traps win on coherence time, lose on gate speed
Ion trap coherence times reach ten hours, but gate operations rely on phonons and are limited by the Paul trap oscillation frequency, making them about a thousand times slower than superconducting. The result is counterintuitive: even if ion traps could scale to code-breaking sizes, cracking 2048-bit RSA would take about a year, while superconducting would take about eight hours. Long coherence time does not mean more work per unit time; for practical computation, slow gate times are a throughput disaster.

2:03:32 The quantum threat is neither tomorrow nor never
A March 2026 paper from Harvard, Caltech, and Qera says ten thousand qubits might break internet encryption, but it would actually take years; even with a hundred thousand physical qubits, under mathematically optimal assumptions, cracking RSA would take about three months. This number strikes at both extreme narratives: the quantum threat is not tomorrow, but it is certainly not forever distant. To achieve 'breakable within months' requires qubit count, gate speed, and error correction all to meet standards simultaneously.

2:50:02 Quantum companies' fate lies in government contracts
HRL lost key project funding in early 2026 and laid off 376 people. Government funding shifted from basic research to applied research demanding rapid commercialization; IBM and Intel received support from the CHIPS Act, and ultimately IBM acquired HRL. Krishna calls this the debut of quantum computing's MVP: quantum companies live or die by government contracts, and being acquired is not failure but a way for the technology to enter an industrial system with manufacturing capability.

3:23:10 A million qubits can't be tuned by hand; it's image recognition
Automated tuning becomes key to scaling: a 2023 paper shows that with only six electrons, manual tuning is possible, but manual tuning of a million qubits would take a human lifetime. Tuning is essentially image recognition—when scanning voltage, tunneling events appear as stripes. Krishna's team uses DETR combined with ResNet and Transformer to automatically recognize stripes and generate parameters. This is also the hidden premise for why silicon spin can reuse semiconductor fabs: no matter how many qubits, software can align them automatically.

3:32:31 Silicon may not be first, but it will be the last to win
FFP's final scores: silicon spin gets 10/10 on qubit quality, 10/10 on control (provided isotope enrichment and valley state issues are solved), and 10000/10 on scalability and economics, for a total of 10020/30; neutral atoms score negative 3000. Krishna admits silicon may not be the first route to achieve fault tolerance, but once it does, it will become the final standard, like transistors replacing vacuum tubes, because it is cheap and easy to manufacture.

item.content:encoded:
Broadcom's president reveals an AI chip roadmap: from a million units to 15 million, with the 'beast' being the largest package of 8 stackable compute dies plus 16 HBM modules, and four of the five frontier labs are collaborating.

Broadcom rarely discloses details, but this time it gave three package tiers and three shipment volumes, plus a clear take on the HBM bottleneck. For those tracking ASICs and packaging, these 11 minutes are more informative than many long analyses.

1:06 Custom chip makers still outsource the last mile
Google, Meta, Amazon, and some frontier model companies can have their own chip design teams, define their own architecture and interconnect, but ultimately they still need to 'get the thing built': dealing with foundries and development kits, managing the timing and latency of connections between transistors. Broadcom is the largest of these fee-based back-end design service providers. Clients come to it not just for design capability but also for a batch of ready-made IP like high-speed I/O, high-performance compute, and memory controllers.

3:09 The most tight-lipped chip company suddenly starts talking
Broadcom is a mystery externally: almost no PR department, rarely proactive disclosures. Occasionally it releases a Tomahawk networking chip or chats with Patrick Kennedy on ServeTheHome. Over the past year, president Charlie has unusually taken the stage to talk about what Broadcom is doing and why it's expanding its customer base from traditional networking chips to custom AI chips. The slide showing three tiers of chips is the clue.

4:09 Today's AI servers are just the smallest tier
Of the three tiers Charlie showed, the leftmost is already shipping in hundreds of thousands of systems, about the size of this Cisco chip on the desk: one compute die in the middle, surrounded by four to six HBM modules, packaged similarly to TSMC's CoWoS. Broadcom says that over the past year, it has shipped more than one million units of this tier for customers. This tier is the reality of today's AI servers.

5:09 Larger packages actually ship in higher volumes
The middle tier is noticeably bigger: two to four compute/I/O dies, surrounded by eight to twelve HBM modules; AMD's MI455X is also in this design form. Charlie's expected shipment volumes are key: the middle tier is expected to ship 5 million units, and the rightmost tier 15 million. Placed next to 'one million in the past year,' this is not linear growth but an order-of-magnitude jump in next-generation AI custom chip shipments.

6:11 The rightmost chip may stack compute dies on compute dies
The rightmost 'beast': the red parts are eight compute dies arranged in two columns of four, and they are stacked. Charlie lifts the red to reveal purple underneath; underneath could be SRAM, or SRAM could be on top; if it's compute-on-compute, it's effectively sixteen compute dies. Each compute die is paired with two HBM modules, so one package has sixteen HBM modules, with two light-blue I/O dies at the top and bottom edges, and openings left at the package edge for optical modules.

7:11 Frontier model companies are almost all building their own chips
Charlie said that of the five most advanced frontier model labs, four are working with Broadcom on custom compute chips. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic define the design they want, Broadcom does the back-end services and interfaces with TSMC, and then partners like Supermicro and WiWynn are brought in for data-center-scale deployment. This also explains why Broadcom is expanding capacity: it's not just serving traditional networking customers but also taking orders from large model companies.

9:11 The bottleneck to scaling may not be packaging but HBM
The real bottleneck may not be packaging but whether there's enough high-bandwidth memory to go around: could a new form between DDR/LPDDR and HBM emerge to fill the gap? Also, Broadcom said on stage that it has already deployed a 2nm chip with a partner, slightly smaller than the beast, and sooner. This reminds us that in the coming years, advanced packaging and HBM capacity will be swept up along with custom chip orders.

10:13 The first 2nm custom chip to land may come from Japan
The host pinned down the 'coming soon, smaller' 2nm chip Broadcom mentioned: he asked George from Chips and Cheese, and the two concluded it's Fujitsu's Monaka—a 2nm compute die paired with a 5nm SRAM die, with a central I/O die in between. This chip has already appeared as a mockup or test silicon at several conferences.

item.title: An Explorer Died for a Fictional City, Born from a Political Forgery
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-stuffmissed-福西特不是去冒险-是去给橡胶资本画地图/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-stuffmissed-福西特不是去冒险-是去给橡胶资本画地图/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Percy Fawcett's Amazon expeditions are often told as adventure legends, but the real starting point was border disputes fueled by the rubber trade; his narrative of 'respect' for indigenous people is a gross oversimplification, and the City of Z that obsessed him may rest on a forged manuscript.
item.content:encoded:
Percy Fawcett's Amazon expeditions are often told as adventure legends, but the real starting point was border disputes fueled by the rubber trade; his narrative of 'respect' for indigenous people is a gross oversimplification, and the City of Z that obsessed him may rest on a forged manuscript.

This episode has moderate information density, but it clearly lays out the beginnings of the rubber trade, indigenous catastrophe, and Manuscript 512; listeners only seeking adventure anecdotes may find the first half's setup a bit long.

3:04 His obsession began with a Roman well in childhood
Fawcett was born in 1867. His family was nominally aristocratic, but his father, Edward Fawcett, had squandered the fortune and could only serve as a private assistant to Queen Victoria's son 'Bertie' (later Edward VII). Fawcett described a loveless childhood in Torquay that made him introverted. His sister recalled that as a child he discovered a well full of Roman pottery on Halden Moors and had his siblings lower him down to retrieve the artifacts and take them to a museum. This boldness, stubbornness, and outward-seeking personality later resurfaced in his fixation on the occult and the Amazon.

8:13 An officer who held séances still rose to major
In 1901 Fawcett married Nina, and in 1903 their first son Jack was born. That same year he was posted to Spike Island off the south coast of Ireland. Fawcett found the posting dull, so he spent his spare time conducting séances. His interest in the occult was not a fringe hobby; his son Brian later wrote that anyone who sought knowledge beyond the material might be called a mystic. This interest did not hinder his military career—he was promoted to major. This shows that Fawcett's 'rationality' and 'superstition' coexisted, setting the stage for his later credulous belief in Manuscript 512.

10:19 His first Amazon trip was a diplomatic mission, not adventure
In 1901 Fawcett joined the Royal Geographical Society and completed specialized training in boundary demarcation. In 1906 the Society's president, Sir George Goldie, met with him and asked about his knowledge of Bolivia, then told him: border disputes among Brazil, Peru, and Bolivia had escalated because of the rubber trade, and the countries involved would not accept demarcation by any interested party, so the Bolivian government asked the Royal Geographical Society to arbitrate and recommend an officer. For Fawcett, this was a chance to 'escape the monotony of an artillery officer's life'; he was 39, and his wife was pregnant with their second child. The chain of argument here is: rubber's economic value → territorial disputes → Britain as a 'disinterested' third party → Fawcett enters the Amazon as a surveyor. The counterintuitive point is that his initial expedition was not self-directed adventure but commercial and diplomatic arrangement.

14:25 He faced attacks everywhere because 90% of natives were already dead
Before he reached South America, the rubber industry had already transformed the region. Figures cited in the episode: before Europeans arrived, the area of present-day Brazil had at least 2,000 indigenous tribes with a total population of about 11 million; in the first hundred years after colonists arrived in the 16th century, 90% of indigenous people died from disease or genocide, and survivors were often enslaved for rubber work. The rubber trade made land extremely valuable, and Europeans moved in and seized indigenous lands, causing natives to view all Europeans as threats—this is the backdrop to Fawcett's encounters with hostility. His own accounts also show he was clearly aware of European colonists' atrocities. This section provides a structural explanation for 'why he was attacked everywhere' and corrects the romanticized narrative of 'explorer in peril.'

17:28 Calling him respectful of natives sets the bar too low
Fawcett's dealings with indigenous people were not solely confrontational. He would insist that he and his companions lay down their arms and show they posed no threat, he learned local languages, and he condemned the earlier European colonists for creating the problems that continued to sour relations. But at the same time, he wrote a great deal that was 'extremely racist' and condescending. The hosts explicitly say that later accounts often describe him as 'respectful of indigenous people,' which is an oversimplification; even if he was 'often better' than his contemporary European explorers, that bar was appallingly low. The value here is that many popular narratives today cast Fawcett as an enlightened explorer, and the episode dismantles that myth with concrete evidence from his writing, without reducing his behavior to that of a pure villain.

19:28 He survived an ambush with an accordion, not a gun
This is one of Fawcett's most famous escape stories. His expedition was ambushed on a river by indigenous archers, and peaceful calls went unanswered. He had his companion Todd sit on a log in the middle of a sandbar with an accordion and start playing, while the others sang loudly and stomped their feet. Before long, the hail of arrows stopped, and a wide-eyed native peered out from the bushes; the expedition was then welcomed into the village and even given help. This example shows Fawcett did not rely solely on force; his tools for problem-solving included music and clownish performance. It also shows that his records contain both observations worth taking seriously and plenty of unreliable exaggeration, setting up contrasts with later descriptions of giant anacondas, peanuts, and double-nosed dogs.

25:32 He believed in a lost city because old documents really described one
Before World War I, Fawcett efficiently completed map surveys (often much faster than expected) while becoming increasingly fascinated by claims of lost cities in the jungle. He named the city he sought 'Zed' and located it in the non-coastal southern Brazilian state of Mato Grosso; that area covers about 900,000 square kilometers, is extremely dense forest, and remains one of Brazil's least densely populated regions even today, with almost no European entry in the early 20th century. The chain of argument here: numerous 16th- and 17th-century Spanish and Portuguese explorer documents described 'very advanced large cities' → Fawcett believed they were real → he became increasingly obsessed with finding the City of Z.

29:40 The manuscript he believed without reservation may be a hoax
After the war, Fawcett continued studying old documents, most often citing Manuscript 512, held in the National Library of Rio de Janeiro: a Portuguese adventurer's 1753 account of his travels in the Amazon, sometimes attributed to one João de Silvestre de Moraes. Fawcett gave the author the pseudonym Francisco Raposo and wrote that he believed the manuscript's contents 'without reservation,' calling it an 'incomparable story.' However, at the start of the episode the hosts had already warned that this document 'is likely a hoax.' So the real suspense is not whether the lost city existed, but why a militarily trained surveyor would become so obsessed with a possibly forged 1753 record.

item.title: Time Is Not an Illusion: Irreversibility Is More Fundamental Than Symmetric Equations
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-mindscape-时间的方向性比时间对称方程更根本/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-mindscape-时间的方向性比时间对称方程更根本/
item.description: Jim Al-Khalili argues that time is real and directed, and that irreversibility is more fundamental than time-symmetric equations; he also proposes using quantum entanglement entropy instead of thermodynamic entropy as the basis for the past hypothesis.
item.content:encoded:
Jim Al-Khalili argues that time is real and directed, and that irreversibility is more fundamental than time-symmetric equations; he also proposes using quantum entanglement entropy instead of thermodynamic entropy as the basis for the past hypothesis.

Sean Carroll and Jim Al-Khalili hold opposing views on the arrow of time, and this episode reveals their real points of disagreement; the second half also covers quantum biology mechanisms and a new hypothesis about quantum entanglement entropy.

4:07 The direction of time is built in, not emergent
Jim takes a hard stance: time is real and tangible, part of four-dimensional spacetime, not just something clocks measure. He goes further, saying that the directionality of time is not emergent from directionless fundamental laws but is built into the universe. Sean reminds the audience that this is highly controversial—many physicists think time is just a tool or that direction is a product of coarse-graining. Jim's intuition is that, seen from inside the universe, irreversibility is the more fundamental thing.

17:38 No system is isolated, so irreversibility is the norm
The traditional narrative is that fundamental equations like Newton's and Schrödinger's are invariant under time reversal, and the arrow of time must emerge from entropy increase or coarse-graining. Jim turns this around: time-symmetric equations are idealizations because no system is truly isolated—even quantum systems are constantly entangled with their environment. Time-symmetric equations apply only to isolated systems and are a special case of the master equation; in reality, everything exchanges energy and information with its surroundings, and irreversibility is the norm. He admits this is a minority view but thinks it is closer to the real world.

27:50 The special moment must be at the Big Bang, not last week
If you treat the whole universe as an isolated system that also obeys time-symmetric laws, then by the second law, yesterday's entropy should be higher than today's, not lower. The only way out is to push that special moment to the very beginning: the Big Bang. That is the past hypothesis. Jim stresses that this is not an extra assumption but part of the universe's initial conditions, on par with the fine-tuning of constants. He agrees with Sean: if you must pick a special moment, the Big Bang is far more reasonable than last week.

31:03 Physical laws contain no flow of time, yet we feel it
Even if low-entropy initial conditions explain the arrow of time, Sean presses: where do psychological experiences like 'now' and the sense of passage come from? Jim honestly admits that physical laws contain no flow of time, yet we feel time flowing. He says this is a gap between physical time and manifest time, and he is not even sure how to articulate it clearly. This frankness is more valuable than pretending it is solved, and it shows the problem of time is far from closed.

45:51 DNA mutations may come from a proton's quantum tunneling
From a nuclear physicist's perspective, Jim presents the most concrete case in quantum biology: the hydrogen bonds between DNA strands are held by hydrogen atoms, which are essentially protons. Löwdin proposed in the early 1960s that a proton might quantum-tunnel through the energy barrier to the opposite strand, causing a mutation during replication. Jim's team has done increasingly refined calculations to determine the ratio of tunneling to thermal excitation. He points out that quantum biology is not the old saw that 'atoms are quantum' but asks whether life has evolved to exploit long-lived coherence and entanglement.

1:03:12 A more fundamental version of the past hypothesis is entanglement entropy
The thermodynamic past hypothesis requires specifying a low-entropy microstate. Jim and philosopher Eddy Chen have tried a more quantum version: assume the universe began in a pure state with extremely low entanglement entropy, with subsystems barely entangled. As it evolves, subsystems become increasingly entangled, and the entanglement entropy of the whole universe rises monotonically. Conceptually this is more fundamental than thermodynamic entropy, but Jim admits there are many gaps—for instance, how finely to partition the subsystems. This direction is still unfinished.

1:12:29 After the heat death of the universe, time still passes
Many say time might disappear at extreme scales. Jim counters: even tens of trillions of years from now, when the universe reaches thermal equilibrium and no change can be used to measure time, time still passes. He admits this is not time in the relativistic sense that holds in every reference frame, but it makes time almost like Newton's absolute clock—a real happening. For him, even if time emerges from something more fundamental, that does not mean it is not real.

item.description: Ahmed Fouad Alkhatib, a policy scholar born in Gaza, argues with four layers of opposition, two polls, and demographic data that most Gazans have long been anti-Hamas and that Hamas may be forced to disarm in stages; but host Russ's pessimism reminds us that disarmament for Hamas equals political suicide.
item.content:encoded:
Ahmed Fouad Alkhatib, a policy scholar born in Gaza, argues with four layers of opposition, two polls, and demographic data that most Gazans have long been anti-Hamas and that Hamas may be forced to disarm in stages; but host Russ's pessimism reminds us that disarmament for Hamas equals political suicide.

This episode offers a rare insider perspective: a Gaza-born scholar argues that Hamas has lost support and may be forced to disarm, and lays out a concrete 100-day zero-violence roadmap; the host's pessimistic skepticism forms a sharp contrast.

8:03 Gazans have responsibility too; occupation cannot be a shield
Alkhatib says he deliberately wrote the book short and colloquial because there is already too much information about Gaza and no one reads long academic texts. The book is written for four audiences: pro-Israel communities, pro-Palestinian communities, Arab and Muslim Americans, and Palestinians themselves. The title is a judgment: Gazans are hostages of Hamas, despite radicalization and peripheral support for some of Hamas's past actions. He asks Palestinians to acknowledge their agency, responsibility, and accountability even under power asymmetry, rather than using 'occupation' or '1948' as a shield. Russ responds that the book is only about 85 pages, yet he, who considers himself well-read on the subject, learned a lot.

18:09 On the day Hamas seized power, he was applying for asylum
Alkhatib was born in 1990, moved back and forth to Gaza with his family in the late 1990s, permanently returned in 2000, and went to the US at age 15 as an exchange student. He remembers the optimism at the end of the Oslo process: his family got their first landline and mobile phone, and he saw state institutions emerge in Gaza. Then came the failure of the Camp David talks in 2000, the outbreak of the Second Intifada, and Gaza turned to another side. On June 14, 2007, the same day Hamas forcibly took over Gaza and drove out the Palestinian Authority, he happened to be interviewing for political asylum and became the first Gazan to receive asylum in the US because of Hamas's control of Gaza. He sees this date coincidence as a synchronization point between his personal fate and Gaza's fate.

21:43 The 2006 election was a gift from America itself
Alkhatib obtained confidential discussion materials from a PLO official: before the 2006 election, the Palestinian Authority explicitly warned the Bush administration and Condoleezza Rice that Hamas would win, but the US still pushed for the election. Hamas leader Zahar allegedly later boasted that they deliberately had supporters underreport their support in Shikaki polls to prevent the US from canceling the election due to high poll numbers. Alkhatib says Shikaki's polls have long been manipulated, and a Hamas document found by the IDF in Gaza in August 2024 shows Hamas was correcting poll results, inflating margins of error to 20% to 40% to exaggerate support. That election transformed Hamas from a resistance movement into a regime ruling Gaza, and was the beginning of the path to October 7.

28:51 Same people, two paths: Gaza builds rockets, West Bank builds a state
This is the framing section of the episode: Gaza and the West Bank became two contrasting experiments after Hamas's takeover. Hamas turned Gaza into an 'armed resistance fortress,' using aid and money from Qatar and Iran to build tunnels and rockets, while outsourcing civilian welfare to the UN and international NGOs; the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank, under Salam Fayyad, built professional security forces and genuine state institutions. Alkhatib's criticism targets both sides: the cost of Hamas goes without saying, while Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu's government, to maintain Palestinian division, allowed settlement expansion and weakened the PA's legitimacy, effectively prolonging Hamas's narrative. He cites the 'South Korea vs. North Korea' analogy: had the West Bank moderates been strongly supported, the trajectory would have been completely different.

36:48 External funding cut off, Hamas has only the path of disarmament
Alkhatib's optimism that Hamas will eventually partially disarm comes from hard constraints: Iran and Hezbollah are preoccupied, Qatar's LNG exports are frozen due to US-Iran conflict, so they can no longer fund Hamas; Hamas has lost most of its experienced fighters and nearly all senior political and military leaders, leaving only the option of accepting 'phased disarmament.' Russ's response is a clear point of disagreement: if the other side knows you want it to disappear, any concession is fake, because disarmament means the end of its control and lifeline. Alkhatib acknowledges there will be militias and tribal revenge, but he believes Gazan society has already distanced itself ideologically from Hamas, and the turning point in the narrative war will come before the political turning point.

44:32 Hamas is a lighter version of ISIS and the Taliban
Alkhatib divides Gazan opposition to Hamas into four layers: the shallowest is 'you destroyed Gaza, we pay for your suicidal nihilism'; the second is Hamas members enriching themselves during the war through aid and overseas fundraising, even bribing their way out of Gaza and then calling from abroad for continued resistance; the third is the entirety of Hamas's twenty-year rule, including suicide bombings and the destruction of the two-state solution; the fourth is the daily oppression by the Interior Ministry, from banning women from smoking hookah on the beach to Sinwar's 2020 attempt to legislate that women need male guardian approval to leave Gaza. His conclusion is direct: Hamas is 'a lighter version of ISIS and the Taliban,' only more concerned with public relations because PR keeps NGO and UN money flowing.

52:36 Poll numbers in a police state are not worth trusting
Russ raises a methodological point: in a police state, poll numbers are meaningless because people dare not tell the truth, so he has always been deeply skeptical of Shikaki polls. Alkhatib offers alternative data: a poll commissioned by the Tony Blair Institute and conducted by Jim Zogby shows 93% of Gazans want Hamas to leave, and 86% hold Hamas equally responsible for Gaza's destruction. Demographics support his judgment: 70% of Gazans have never left Gaza, and nearly two-thirds of the population is under 30, having only experienced Hamas rule and knowing the world through smartphones. He believes the largest group is not ideological resisters but ordinary people driven by economic interests, who are the most reliable foundation for peace.

54:18 The danger is not Gazans but the organization Hamas
Regarding the argument that 'some of the October 7 attackers had worked in Israel and received medical treatment, yet betrayed those who treated them well,' Alkhatib acknowledges that from a pre-war population of 2.3 million, they were a minority, but the problem is not individual cases but structure: as long as Hamas retains the capability to gather intelligence, recruit, and launch attacks, any interaction can be exploited under coercion. Once Gaza achieves disarmament and transitional governance, the risk will not go to zero but will drop exponentially to a manageable level. Russ uses the post-war demilitarization of Japan and Germany as positive historical cases, but doubts whether the external management conditions can be met this time. The core disagreement shifts from 'Can Gazans be trusted?' to 'Will the organization Hamas completely disappear?'

item.title: US Economic Resilience Comes from Consumers Borrowing from the Future
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-oddlots-美国经济韧性来自消费者向未来借钱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-oddlots-美国经济韧性来自消费者向未来借钱/
item.description: Barkin explains why consumption stays strong despite high prices: consumers cut savings, skip bills, and delay loan payments to keep spending; AI investment so far is more about price hikes and crowding out than productivity gains; the Fed may face a long headwind.
item.content:encoded:
Barkin explains why consumption stays strong despite high prices: consumers cut savings, skip bills, and delay loan payments to keep spending; AI investment so far is more about price hikes and crowding out than productivity gains; the Fed may face a long headwind.

Micro-evidence from the front lines as heard by a Fed official: consumers sustain spending by borrowing from the future, AI construction crowds out traditional building, and tariff refunds boost profits. Useful for calibrating macro views on US inflation stickiness and AI capital spending.

3:05 You can't find forward guidance from someone who doesn't give it
Asked about Warsh's speech at Jackson Hole, Barkin said he listened carefully but explicitly refused to infer September FOMC action from it. "He doesn't like forward guidance, so you shouldn't look for forward guidance from someone who doesn't give it." Barkin stressed that one can discuss the economy well, but if you choose not to give forward guidance, you don't. This remark also addresses the market's tendency to try to extract the rate path from any Fed official comment. He described this impulse as "we can't help but want to know," but argued it should be restrained.

4:06 Consumers' money is borrowed from the future
Barkin's observation: unlike the Great Recession, during the pandemic people accumulated lots of cash, stocks, and home equity, and developed a "I'm going to spend" mindset. Crucially, lower-income consumers are also "creatively finding money": shifting to Walmart and dollar stores, cutting insurance, having kids move back home, not paying summer gas bills, and letting car loans run 60 days past due instead of 120—essentially "borrowing from the future." His conclusion: as long as employment and asset markets are healthy, spending sustained by lower savings and skipped bills will continue. This micro mechanism explains the economy's "resilience" better than macro data.

6:08 Data centers crowd ordinary construction out of the building cycle
Early in the year, $700 billion in investment was announced in a single week, and transformers, switchgear, and electricians are all in short supply. Barkin believes the construction cycle is shifting from office and multifamily housing to data centers and industrial; multifamily "doesn't pencil out" can't be blamed solely on rates, because in 2004-05 when rates were similarly high, there was still plenty of building. He acknowledged that data center construction does push up costs for other construction, creating a "chicken-and-egg" crowding-out effect, but it's hard to say precisely to what degree. This answer soberly shows the real internal disagreement about the spillover effects of AI capex.

8:10 AI first affects hiring, not output
At every chamber of commerce and town hall, Barkin hears AI questions that are political: jobs, water, data centers. Economically, AI's productivity shock is still confined to a few substitutable scenarios like call centers, programming, and clerical work; current productivity gains come more from automation and process reengineering driven by the 2022 labor shortage. On the hiring side, employers are already using the logic of "can AI do it first, then decide whether to hire" to restrain hiring. The enthusiasm of firms and workers is asymmetric: bosses are active, employees are lukewarm. That is, AI currently affects the economy by reducing employment demand rather than boosting output.

16:17 Choosing an inflation narrative is choosing a rate path
Barkin framed today's inflation as two readings. One is "65 months below target, no excuses," corresponding to Warsh's hawkish stance: inflation has been above target for a long time, and rates may not be tight enough. The other is "47 months up plus 18 months down": inflation emerged after the pandemic, and after rate hikes it had fallen to 2.3%-2.4% by March 2025, only to be pushed back up by AI, tariffs, and oil shocks. He explicitly said the second "is perfectly defensible," and "we will bring it back down later." Which narrative prevails determines whether the Fed keeps tightening or waits for shocks to fade.

17:20 Tariffs are now a stimulus because refunds have arrived
The tariff topic is quieter than six months ago, not because trade is less important, but because refunds have arrived after the Supreme Court ruling. Barkin said that over the past three or four months, companies have been receiving refunds rather than paying extra tariffs. Steel and aluminum producers benefit from tariffs as a "price umbrella"; foreign manufacturers that ship European parts to the US for assembly are instead hurt by tariffs. Refunds are "very positive" for corporate profits, and companies use them for marketing, store renovations, and maintaining hiring, so they have a stimulative effect, but the pass-through to prices is "very targeted," not systemic. This explains why people are complaining less about tariffs now.

21:25 Data centers' tax base buys no political goodwill
Local residents resent data centers because, unlike factories, they don't have workers' kids playing ball with local children; the tax base benefits touted by economic developers lack political resonance. Barkin half-joked that they should name an elementary school after Microsoft or Google to win hearts. He admitted he doesn't know how large data centers will become; AI footprint, data center footprint, and energy demand could all be significantly under- or overestimated. If political backlash leads to underbuilding, it will drag on growth; if overbuilding, it will add to inflation. This is an uncertainty not yet incorporated into the policy framework.

24:30 AI could be inflationary or deflationary; don't bet early
On whether AI brings a productivity boom and raises the neutral rate R-star, Barkin is cautious. He said the AI path one, two, or three years out has an "extremely wide range," and could manifest as inflation or deflation, with 18 versions in between. Until there is enough confidence, policy cannot be based on assumptions. He also responded to Warsh's view: different AI model simulations point to completely opposite rate directions. Therefore, he hinted the Fed should wait for data rather than put AI productivity into the dot plot ahead of time. This stance is a warning to those betting on a higher R-star.
